title: 402 garment factories shut  in Bangladesh over three years
President expects favourable SC ruling on controversial 22nd Amendment | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 05:58
-     - 0

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake said the 22nd Amendment to the Constitution would be approved by Parliament soon after the Supreme Court communicates its determination to the Speaker, addressing a public rally in Bulathsinhala.

The President said the proposed Amendment was essential to strengthen measures against corruption, and that the Government had taken steps to expedite the judicial process, including recruiting additional judicial service personnel, speeding up reports from the Government Analyst’s Department, and establishing more High Courts to clear the backlog of pending cases.

“Immediately after the determination, we will take it to Parliament and pass it,” he said.

The proposed 22nd Amendment to the Constitution seeks to extend the retirement age of higher court judges, a move opposed by the legal fraternity including the Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL). 

Last week, the Supreme Court heard a record 64 petitions against the proposed constitutional change and said its judgement would be communicated to the Speaker of Parliament.

President Dissanayake said some cases had remained unresolved for 15 to 20 years, resulting in the current wave of arrests as authorities worked through the backlog. 

“Some claim that we are carrying out political revenge. If there had been no backlog of cases, there would not be this many arrests,” President Dissanayake said.

He further claimed that if all alleged corruption and wrongdoing uncovered by the Government were fully investigated, few of those responsible would remain untouched, saying the scale of alleged wrongdoing had become apparent only after the Government examined State affairs from within. 

“If you look at the reality, it is almost to the extent that not a single person would be left,” he said, referring to those he accused of past corruption and wrongdoing.

President Dissanayake said the Government would proceed with constitutional and legal reforms despite opposition, alleging that beneficiaries of what he described as a “black State” were increasingly concerned, and that opponents of the reforms were approaching foreign embassies and writing to international organisations. 

“They should be worried. But remember, the decisions we take are carefully considered and taken on behalf of the people. We will not reverse any such decision,” he said.

On the black economy, President Dissanayake said action by the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and Sri Lanka Customs had curbed illegal dollar outflows, claiming approximately $ 1 billion had been illegally moved out of the country, an amount he compared to Sri Lanka’s annual tea export earnings. 

He said measures had also been taken to prevent State revenue being diverted before reaching the Treasury or misused thereafter. “We closed all those routes and ensured that every cent that should come to the Treasury comes to the Treasury,” he said.

On fiscal matters, President Dissanayake said Government revenue reached 16.7% of GDP in 2025, the highest level in around three decades, and that Sri Lanka had recorded its lowest Budget deficit since 1957, attributing the improvement to higher revenue and tighter expenditure control. 

He criticised previous governments for undertaking major infrastructure projects, including ports and airports, without adequate assessments.

Looking ahead, he said the Government planned to allocate Rs. 2 trillion for capital expenditure next year, describing it as an unprecedented level of development spending, alongside a Rs. 2 billion budgetary reserve for each district to be used for local priorities with District Coordinating Committees and District Secretaries. 

He also cited increases in welfare payments, including the Mahapola scholarship allowance, the fertiliser subsidy, and allowances for elderly people and persons with disabilities.

title: Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh to visit Sri Lanka tomorrow | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 05:56
-     - 5

Rajnath Singh

Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh will undertake an official visit to Sri Lanka from 8 to 10 September, according to a statement issued by the Press Information Bureau (PIB) in Delhi on behalf of India’s Defence Ministry.

Singh will hold consultations with Sri Lanka’s leadership on a range of issues during the visit and interact separately with the Indian diaspora in Colombo, the statement said. He will lead a high-level delegation comprising senior officials from India’s Defence Ministry and External Affairs Ministry.

The statement described India and Sri Lanka as sharing deep civilisational ties and a multifaceted partnership anchored by regional security, defence, economic and trade cooperation, and strong people-to-people ties. It pointed to India’s assistance to Sri Lanka during the island’s economic crisis, and its role as one of the first responders following Cyclone Ditwah in 2025, as having provided further impetus to the bilateral relationship.

The visit was framed by New Delhi as reflecting India’s continued commitment to its ‘Neighbourhood First’ Policy and Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s MAHASAGAR vision, an acronym for Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions. 

The Defence Ministry statement said the visit would further strengthen bilateral relations in mutually beneficial areas, including a strong maritime and defence partnership.

title: Deputy Minister rejects claims of shifting tax terms at Port City after investor backlash | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 05:56
-     - 12

Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Deputy Minister Chathuranga Abeysinghe was drawn into a public dispute on LinkedIn over the past day after a technology entrepreneur accused the Government of repeatedly changing the tax terms offered to companies registering at the Colombo Port City Special Economic Zone (SEZ).

The exchange was triggered by a post from Shavini Fernando, Founder of a Virtual Reality (VR) and web design and development firm, who said her company applied to register at Port City last year after being told employees and companies would face zero tax for three years, prompting her to set up a local office rather than continue engaging staff as consultants. She said applications, including hers, were subsequently held pending changes to the law, after which she was told in a meeting with Port City officials last December that employees would pay 15% and the company 7%, terms she accepted before completing registration.

Fernando said those terms have since changed again, with employees now facing the same 36% income tax rate applied to companies operating from the Sri Lankan mainland, eliminating the incentive that had drawn her to register in the first place. 

“You are ripping off investors,” she wrote, adding that she was reconsidering the arrangement and might instead consolidate operations in Dubai.

Responding on the same thread, Deputy Minister Abeysinghe pushed back on the characterisation of the matter as a personal negotiation, saying Port City investors, including Fernando, had been briefed on the change in law by the Port City Commission, and that close to 90 applications had been held pending its amendment. He said the revised law was unambiguous, with all individuals taxed under the Inland Revenue Act and “no arbitrage between Port City and main land.” In a later reply, Abeysinghe apologised for the confusion, saying his general understanding was that individuals earning foreign income are taxed at 15%, and that further clarity on how the rule applies to Port City’s Approved Persons would be provided.

The confusion appears rooted in how income is classified once received. Corporate finance professional Rasanja Perera, also commenting on the thread, noted that under the mainland tax structure, foreign income received into a Sri Lankan bank account in foreign currency is taxed at 15%, while income treated as local is taxed at 36%, a distinction he said applies at Port City as well. Fernando said her dispute centred on exactly this point, as payments processed through her company’s US dollar account were being treated as local income and taxed at the higher rate.

The thread drew wider commentary from other investors and professionals questioning Port City’s competitiveness against rival free zones. One user cited the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), where corporate tax falls from 25% to zero, as an example of the kind of certainty Sri Lanka would need to offer to attract capital, while others, including a corporate lawyer who has separately written on the subject, said similar concerns were being raised by other current and prospective Port City investors over the zone’s value proposition relative to regional peers.

title: Related-party guarantee rules for banks eased, reporting requirement tightened | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 05:26
-     - 8

The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) has loosened the terms under which licensed banks may rely on corporate guarantees when lending to related parties, while allowing machinery to be pledged as collateral for the first time, under a revised Determination on insider lending.

Banking Act Determination No. 01 of 2026, dated 28 August 2026, takes effect from 1 September 2026, replacing Determination No. 04 of 2024 and its 2025 amendment. It was issued under Sections 47 and 76K of the Banking Act, No. 30 of 1988, as amended. 

Signed by CBSL Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe, the directive said the rules were intended to mitigate potential conflicts of interest and prevent banks from extending more favourable treatment to related parties.

The clearest change is to corporate guarantees. Previously, a guarantee from a third-party concern could cover only 80% of a related-party loan where the guarantor was rated ‘AAA’ to ‘AA-,’ dropping to 60% for guarantors rated ‘A+’ to ‘BBB-.’ That tiered structure has now been scrapped. 

Under the new Determination, any guarantor rated ‘BBB-’ or above, the lowest rung of investment grade, can back the full 100% of the loan.

A second change adds an entirely new collateral category that did not exist before: mortgages over machinery, capped at 50% of the asset’s value as determined by an external valuation obtained within six months of the loan being granted, subject to periodic review under Board-approved internal valuation policies.

A third change applies specifically to the public sector. Where a licensed bank lends to Ministries, Departments of the Government of Sri Lanka, or State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs), it may now accept a letter of undertaking or other instrument issued by the General Treasury instead of conventional security, provided the instrument confirms adequate budget provision for the liability and is disclosed in the Government’s financial statements as a commitment. This option was absent from the 2024 rules.

Reporting requirements have also been tightened procedurally. Banks previously reported related-party transactions quarterly, from the quarter ended 31 December 2024, in a format left unspecified by the CBSL. Under the new rules, reporting begins from the quarter ending 30 September 2026, through two specifically named web-based FinNet returns, BSD-QF-06-RPC and BSD-QF-06-RPI.

Every other collateral ratio in the framework is unchanged, including Government or CBSL securities at 90% of value, cash deposits at 90%, gold at 70%, freehold property with a primary mortgage at 80% of forced sale value, Colombo Stock Exchange-listed shares at 50%, corporate debentures rated ‘AAA’ to ‘BBB-’ at 50%, and life insurance policies at 75% of surrender value.

One provision carries over unaltered: a company that becomes a related party solely because a director or partner also sits on the bank’s board may still borrow under a standard loan agreement, provided it commits the borrower to furnish approved collateral within 90 calendar days if its credit quality deteriorates to Stage 3 under Banking Act Direction No. 13 of 2021.

title: UNP marks 80 years with renewed focus on sovereignty, democracy and political unity | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 05:24
-     - 11

The United National Party (UNP), one of Sri Lanka's oldest political movements, marked its 80th anniversary yesterday (6), with its leadership and representatives of several Opposition parties reflecting on the party’s political legacy, whilst warning of challenges to democracy and the country’s constitutional order.

Addressing the anniversary event, former President and UNP leader Ranil Wickremesinghe said the party, founded on 6 September 1946 under the leadership of D. S. Senanayake should use its 80th anniversary to begin shaping a modern political organisation capable of addressing the needs of the 21st century.

He outlined plans for a "modern UNP" to be unveiled in December, timed to the 120th birth anniversary of former President J.R. Jayewardene. 

“The modern UNP will emerge at that time. I hope to shape the ideologies of the modern UNP according to the ideas it has today, add new faces, and create a Sri Lanka that is fit for the 21st century,” he said.

Wickremesinghe noted that several of the party’s founding members were no longer alive, but their political legacy continued through their children and grandchildren, including within other political parties.

“One of the founding members was D. A. Rajapaksa. Two of his sons served as Presidents of this country,” he said.

Wickremesinghe said the theme of the anniversary program was “Sovereignty”, tracing its development from independence in 1948 through the republican constitutions of 1972 and 1978.

He argued that the 1978 Constitution had established the principle that sovereignty belongs to the people and could not be alienated, with legislature, the executive and the judiciary exercising that sovereignty through the constitutional framework.

Wickremesinghe said the protection of that principle had become particularly important amid what he described as restrictions on political parties, arrests of politicians and pressure on trade unions and professional groups.

“The biggest threat to this system is the non-recognition of the sovereignty of the people,” he claimed.

He also criticised attempts to weaken independent institutions, alleging that the Government was targeting the Bar Association, doctors, and the Buddhist clergy. 

"Where is this country governed? From Parliament or from Pelawatte?" Wickremesinghe asked, charging all of this is destroying the country’s constitution and the sovereignty of the people.  

He called for political forces to come together to protect the constitutional principle of popular sovereignty.

He also condemned the arrest of Sri Lanka Podujana Peramuna (SLPP) National Organiser and MP Namal Rajapaksa, grandson of founding member D.A. Rajapaksa, whom he had personally invited to the celebration. 

“Unfortunately, Namal Rajapaksa was arrested,” Wickremesinghe said, adding that he and the UNP strongly opposed the action.

People’s United Opposition convener Prof. G. L. Peiris said sovereignty was key to Sri Lanka’s democratic system, arguing that fundamental changes to the Constitution should be subject to the direct approval of the people.

He recalled that the country’s sovereignty had been held by foreign powers for centuries before independence in 1948, and said the constitutional development that followed ultimately placed sovereignty directly with the people.

Peiris said the 1972 Constitution transferred sovereignty to the Council of State, while the 1978 Constitution went further by vesting sovereignty directly in the people rather than their representatives.

“Under the current constitution, sovereignty is very clearly vested in the people. It is practically exercised through a referendum,” he said.

While Parliament has the power to make laws, Prof. Peiris said that power was not absolute, where fundamental constitutional principles were concerned.

“In matters that are of utmost importance to the people, in changing the basic features of the Constitution, the opinion of the people should be obtained directly, not through members of Parliament,” he said.

He stressed the importance of judicial independence, arguing that any fundamental change affecting it should also require a referendum.

“If a government wrongly usurps the sovereignty of the people, a future government inevitably has a responsibility to correct that situation and return the sovereignty that was taken away to the people,” Prof. Peiris said.

Sri Lanka Freedom Party (SLFP) Chairman Nimal Siripala de Silva offered cross-party tribute, crediting the UNP's historical contributions from D.S. Senanayake's agricultural colonisation schemes to Ranasinghe Premadasa's garment factories and Gam Udawa housing program, to J.R. Jayewardene's open economy. 

He highlighted D. S. Senanayake’s agricultural development program, including the establishment of farming colonies in previously underdeveloped areas, as well as the economic and social programs introduced by successive UNP governments.

He credited late President Ranasinghe Premadasa with establishing around 300 garment factories and promoting export-oriented employment, while also highlighting the Gam Udawa program.

de Silva said J. R. Jayewardene’s introduction of the open economy had taken the country in a new direction, noting that successive governments had subsequently adopted policies aimed at strengthening the private sector.

He singled out Wickremesinghe's economic stewardship in 2022, at a time when the country was facing severe shortages of foreign exchange and essential commodities.

“When the country was bankrupt and ran out of dollars, when the people were unable to get gas and oil and when everyone rejected him, he took over the leadership of this country. Wickremesinghe, without thinking about his political journey,” de Silva said. 

He acknowledged that Wickremesinghe made many difficult decisions to stabilise the economy before handing over the country to the present administration with $ 6 billion in the Government coffers.

de Silva also recalled that the SLFP itself had emerged from the UNP, noting that S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike had left the UNP to pursue what he regarded as a more progressive political path.

While acknowledging ideological differences, he called for politics to remain centred on competing ideas rather than hostility. "Politics is not hate politics, but democracy is only ideological politics."

Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB) General Secretary Ranjith Madduma Bandara delivered the historically detailed remarks, recounting the UNP's founding at Colombo's Farm Court House in 1946, where D.S. Senanayake declared it "a party that belongs to all races." 

He listed the party's achievements; the Gal Oya, Minipe and Mahaweli irrigation projects, free trade zones, and the extension of free education.

Bandara said the UNP had to face the 1971 rebellion against democracy, the JVP 1988-1989 conflict, and the 30 years' civil conflict to protect the country's freedom and democracy, referring to the deaths of leaders including; Ranasinghe Premadasa, Gamini Dissanayake and Lalith Athulathmudali, as well as thousands of party members.

“The party had lost leaders, and six to seven thousand party members also sacrificed their lives,” he added. 

He said the country was again facing a challenge to democratic institutions, arguing that the balance among the legislature, executive and judiciary had weakened.

“The 22nd Amendment is working to destroy the independence of the judiciary and the country’s democracy,” Bandara claimed.

Noting that the UNP and SJB, both descended from the same political lineage, he said political forces should set aside differences in the interests of protecting democracy.

“Many of the policies of the UNP are the same as our policies. I also started politics with the UNP and today I am working for the SJB. At this important time, the UNP and the SJB should unite again,” Bandara said.

title: FCCISL, Chathura open talks to drive SMEs toward 25% export growth | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 05:22
-     - 14

FCCISL delegation including President Dr. M. Rohitha Silva (fourth from left) with Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Deputy Minister Chathuranga Abeysinghe

The Federation of Chambers of Commerce and Industry of Sri Lanka (FCCISL) held a high-level bilateral policy dialogue with Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Deputy Minister Chathuranga Abeysinghe last week. 

The meeting established a unified roadmap to accelerate regional enterprise growth and integrate the private sector with the government’s newly launched National SME Strategy Framework, aligning with the strategic vision created by the FCCISL Strategy and State Affairs Committees.

Led by FCCISL President Dr. M. Rohitha Silva, the delegation presented a comprehensive blueprint to identify, incubate, and develop between 1,000 and 5,000 scalable Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) across all districts and provinces. This nationwide rollout will be executed in direct collaboration with the Ministry and its affiliated state agencies. The program focuses on transformational growth, an integrated approach, market orientation, fostering an entrepreneurial society, and delivering measurable outcomes and impact, operating directly in line with the Ministry’s vision. To achieve policy goals in earnings, exports, employment, competitiveness, and sustainability, FCCISL and the Ministry will implement joint approaches in institutional strengthening, capability enhancement, growth enablement, and problem-solving.

Leveraging its nine regional pillars, 65 affiliated chambers, and international chamber alliances, the FCCISL will shortly launch a three-year roadmap. This initiative will strengthen the private sector, supporting growth and a sustainable circular economy integrated with government policies.

To drive rapid export expansion and strategic import substitution, the partnership will establish localised incubation systems focused on high-priority economic sectors. Target industries include Agriculture and Food Security, Information and Communication Technology (ICT), Transport and Logistics, Eco-friendly Products, Seafood, and Value-added Coconut and Rubber products.

Furthermore, to ensure these scalable enterprises can access international supply chains, FCCISL outlined its “SMEs Go Global” initiative. This program will leverage the Federation’s strong institutional ties with global commerce bodies—including the SAARC Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the Confederation of Asia-Pacific Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CACCI), APTA CCI, the European Union (EU), and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC)—to facilitate direct market entry for Sri Lankan exporters.

In alignment with this global outreach strategy, the FCCISL formally invited the Deputy Minister to participate in upcoming international trade and investment missions. These include a collaborative delegation to India with FICCI, a bilateral trade visit to New Zealand, and a targeted Investment Forum with Saudi Arabia scheduled for early 2027.

Addressing structural capital requirements, both institutions strategised on unlocking specialised government funding mechanisms to support key sectors. Discussions highlighted the mobilisation of the Construction Guarantee Fund to stabilise the construction sector, alongside dedicated financial instruments for ICT ventures and emerging startups.

FCCISL President Dr. M. Rohitha Silva said: “This partnership marks a critical step in bridging national industrial policy with grassroots enterprise development,” stated “By aligning our regional chamber network directly with the SME Nexus framework and unlocking international market corridors, we are building an actionable, scalable ecosystem that will transform localised businesses into globally competitive entities.”

The FCCISL delegation included Past President Shirley Jayawardane; State Affairs Committee Chairman Ruwan De Silva; Risk and Sustainability Committee Chairman Dhammika Lokuge; Strategy Committee Co-Chairman Thusith Wijesinghe; Director Dr. Vignesh Kularatnam; Secretary-General Tilan M. Wijesooriya; and Head of Operations M. I. S. Fathima.

title: Sri Lanka – Benelux Business Council holds 31st AGM | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 05:21
-     - 11

Seated from left: Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands to Sri Lanka and Maldives Deputy Ambassador/Head of Economic Department Iwan Rutjens, Ambassador Wiebe de Boer, SLBBC President Farhath Amith, Senior Vice President Mr. Shameel Mohideen, and The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce Secretary General/CEO Shiran Fernando. Standing from left: The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce Secretariat Pasandi Senara, Hiwin Chandrasekara, Dr. D S K Pathirana, P. M. Abeysekara, Honorary Consul to Luxembourg Suwaneetha Senanayake, Department of Commerce Acting Director General of Commerce Somasena Mahadiulwewa, Andre Fernando, and Asela Samarapperuma

The Sri Lanka – Benelux Business Council (SLBBC) of The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce conducted its 31st Annual General Meeting recently.

Chief Guest Ambassador of the Kingdom of the Netherlands to Sri Lanka and the Maldives Wiebe de Boer, during his address, highlighted the enduring relevance of the Benelux union as a sandbox for further European Intergration – including its role in linking Sri Lankan exporters to the Port of Rotterdam. The Ambassador confirmed that Sri Lanka’s GSP+ access remains in place until 2029, with a two-year window to reapply under a new regime, and expressed hope that Sri Lanka could eventually progress from GSP+ to a full Free Trade Agreement with the EU, similar to the EU-India FTA signed this year. He also raised concerns over bureaucratic hurdles facing entrepreneurs, citing delays in quality-control clearances and restrictive foreign investment caps. 

President of the Council Mr. Farhath Amith reaffirmed the Council’s commitment to strengthening Sri Lanka – Benelux trade and investment ties, calling for continued Benelux support to extend Sri Lanka’s GSP+ status by a further five years. He highlighted key sectors for greater collaboration, including renewable energy (targeting 70% renewable electricity generation by 2030), floriculture, agriculture and agro-processing (including GI-certifiable crops such as cocoa and vanilla), eco-tourism, the coconut industry, and healthcare. He also called for a long-overdue business promotion mission to the Netherlands.

The President highlighted that the process of selecting Sri Lankan spices and agricultural commodities for GI Certification has been very slow over the years, causing the country to miss out on expanding export market opportunities to the EU. He noted that there is no delay on the part of Sri Lanka’s regulatory and competent authorities in supporting stakeholder GI authorities with the required information.

He further highlighted that, with the Netherlands serving as the gateway for the floriculture industry in the EU, Sri Lanka should be considered as the hub in South Asia for the tropical ornamental plants and cut-foliage trade.

Fanam International Ltd., Director Farhath Amith was re-elected President for the 2026/2027 term, while Spillburg Holdings Ltd.’s Shaameel Mohideen and Vinu International Trading Company Ltd.’s P.M. Abeysekara were reappointed Senior Vice President and Vice President respectively. The Council also elected committee members representing Andrew The Travel Company Ltd., MAC Holdings Ltd., Maliban Healthcare Ltd., Propylon One Ltd., Sri Lanka Technology Development Corporate Society, and Thames International Educational Consultancy Ltd., Aitken Spence Travels Ltd., Assistant Vice President Sajith Wijenayake will continue to serve on the Committee as Immediate Past President.

title: CCWE National Workshop calls for collective action to strengthen women’s economic empowerment | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 05:18
-     - 9

Industrial Development Board Chairman Yasas Hewage (left) with AFD Deputy Director for Sri Lanka Amelie July and Ceylon Chamber of Women Entrepreneurs President Dr. Ayanthi Gurusinghe

The Ceylon Chamber of Women Entrepreneurs (CCWE), in collaboration with the University of Kelaniya, brought together policymakers, development partners, private-sector leaders, academics, civil society organisations and women entrepreneurs at the National Workshop “Advocating for Change: Women’s Economic Empowerment through Collective Action.”

The workshop formed part of the FAME – Feminism: Action and Mobilisation for an Inclusive Economy Project, supported by the Agence Française de Développement (AFD), and focused on identifying practical pathways to create a more inclusive and enabling entrepreneurial ecosystem for women in Sri Lanka.

The national dialogue provided a platform to bring together policy-level perspectives with the experiences of women entrepreneurs and grassroots organisations, while presenting research evidence on the barriers, opportunities and institutional changes required to strengthen women’s participation in entrepreneurship and economic development.

Welcoming participants, Ceylon Chamber of Women Entrepreneurs President Dr. Ayanthi Gurusinghe emphasised that women’s economic empowerment cannot be achieved through isolated interventions or training programs alone. She highlighted the importance of connecting women entrepreneurs with finance, technology, markets, knowledge, networks and policy-making institutions, while ensuring that the voices of women at community level are represented in national discussions. She noted that the purpose of “Advocating for Change” is to bring these different voices together and move from identifying challenges towards practical and sustainable solutions.

Dr. Gurusinghe further stressed the importance of collective action among government institutions, development partners, academia, the private sector, women’s chambers and community organisations to create meaningful economic opportunities for women across Sri Lanka.

Partnerships for progress – France’s continued support for women’s economic empowerment 

Embassy of France Deputy Ambassador Matthieu John highlighted the importance of partnerships in advancing inclusive economic development and reflected on the contribution of the FAME partnership in Sri Lanka.

He emphasised the value of strengthening women’s participation in economic decision-making and creating opportunities that enable women not only to establish enterprises but also to build sustainable businesses capable of contributing to employment, innovation and economic growth. The participation of France and AFD in the program reinforced the importance of international development partnerships that support locally led initiatives, research, advocacy and collective action for women’s economic empowerment.

Creating an enabling ecosystem for women entrepreneurs 

Delivering the keynote address,  Industrial Development Board (IDB) Chairman Yasas Hewage, focused on the importance of creating an enabling ecosystem in which women entrepreneurs can move beyond micro and livelihood-based enterprises towards sustainable, growth-oriented businesses.He highlighted the role of enterprise-development institutions in providing entrepreneurs with access to technical knowledge, technology, productivity improvement, business-development services, finance and markets.

Hewage also emphasised that strengthening women-owned enterprises should be viewed not merely as a gender or social-development intervention, but as an important component of Sri Lanka’s wider industrial and economic development

Panel 1 – From Policy to Progress: Building an enabling ecosystem for women entrepreneurs

This brought together government, development partners, the private sector and women entrepreneurs to examine how Sri Lanka can create a stronger enabling environment for women-owned businesses. The discussion featured Women and Child Affairs Ministry Deputy Director - Development Jayanthi Hewakuruppu, IAS Holdings Ltd., Group Managing Director Tania Polonnowita Wettimuny, DAZZLE Founder and CEO Niluka Weligamage, and Agence Française de Développement (AFD) Gender Specialist Juliette Van Wassenhove.

The first panel brought together representatives from the Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Ministry, Women and Child Affairs Ministry, private sector and Agence Française de Développement (AFD) to examine how policy and institutional mechanisms can better support women entrepreneurs.

The panel called for a shift “from policy to progress”, with stronger coordination between government, development partners, financial institutions and the private sector. The key outcome was the need to ensure that policies and programs deliver measurable results for women entrepreneurs—particularly improved business sustainability, income, productivity, employment creation, market access and opportunities to scale from micro enterprises into competitive and sustainable businesses.

Panel 2 – Voices from the ground: Women leading change through collective action 

This panel brought grassroots realities into the national dialogue through CPWCIC President Kanthi Mdagammana, DDS President Nilanthi Perera, RRWO President Daya Dadallage, and KNDS President Ramya Kumuduni. The speakers shared the experiences of women entrepreneurs working at community and provincial levels, particularly outside Sri Lanka’s main commercial centres.

The panel strongly called for a bottom-up approach to policy development, ensuring that the voices and lived experiences of women entrepreneurs from different provinces are directly reflected in national decision-making. A central outcome was the recognition that women entrepreneurs should not simply be beneficiaries of programs, but active partners in designing, implementing and evaluating policies that affect their businesses and economic participation. Strengthening collective action and linking grassroots organisations more closely with national institutions were identified as essential to achieving sustainable change.

Evidence for change 

Presenting the research findings, University of Kelaniya Department of Social Statistics Professor and Centre for Gender Studies Acting Director Prof. Sanika Sulochani Ramanayake, presented evidence on the barriers and opportunities affecting women entrepreneurs and the pathways required to strengthen women’s economic participation.

The findings highlighted the importance of moving towards an ecosystem approach in which access to finance, skills, technology, formalisation, markets, networks and institutional support are interconnected rather than delivered as isolated interventions.

The research also reinforced the importance of evidence-based advocacy and of ensuring that the experiences of women entrepreneurs from different regions and economic backgrounds are reflected in future policy discussions.

From dialogue to action

The National Workshop concluded with a call for stronger coordination and continued collective action among government, development partners, financial institutions, academia, the private sector, women’s organisations and entrepreneurs.

Among the broader priorities emerging from the dialogue were the need to strengthen access to finance and markets; improve technology, digital and business-development support; create stronger pathways from micro-enterprise to sustainable business growth; strengthen institutional coordination; improve access to opportunities for women outside Colombo; and ensure that women entrepreneurs have a stronger voice in policy and economic decision-making.

CCWE emphasised that the dialogue is intended to contribute to a wider process of evidence-based advocacy for women’s economic empowerment, ensuring that recommendations are informed not only by research and institutional perspectives but also by the lived experiences of women entrepreneurs themselves.

The workshop reaffirmed a central message: Women’s economic empowerment is not solely a women’s issue—it is fundamental to Sri Lanka’s inclusive economic growth, industrial development and long-term prosperity.

Through “Advocating for Change: Women’s Economic Empowerment through Collective Action,” CCWE and its partners will continue to work towards transforming dialogue and evidence into practical recommendations and stronger collective action for women entrepreneurs across Sri Lanka.

title: Ex-Ceylon Chamber staff celebrate 10th anniversary bash | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 7 September 2026 05:15
-     - 13

Puvi Domingopillai (second from left) with the organising committee after the presentation

The Ex-Ceylon Chamber of Commerce Employees marked their 10th anniversary bash with a lively celebration at the ME Hotel, Colombo, recently. The wellattended event brought together former colleagues for an evening of camaraderie, games, and dancing.

A highlight of the evening was the presentation of a Plaque of Recognition to Puvi Domingopillai, former Senior Assistant Secretary General of the Chamber. Domingopillai was honored for her vision and steadfast support in initiating and sustaining the reunion bash over the past decade.

Guests enjoyed reminiscing about shared experiences, rekindling friendships, and celebrating the enduring spirit of the Chamber community.
